Definition: Percentage of mobile connections using smartphones (as opposed to feature phones or basic phones). Smartphones are the minimum device requirement for accessing most digital public infrastructure services, apps, and mobile internet.
Comments: No GSMA smartphone adoption (% connections smartphones) primary figure retrieved; only media commentary without underlying report access.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Fast-path check (single search) surfaced a GSMA-authored, Nigeria-specific report, so the row was moved to the full path rather than confirmed as Unknown. GSMA's 'AI for Africa: Nigeria deep dive' (August 2024, using GSMA Intelligence data) states smartphone adoption was 51% of mobile connections in 2022, projected to reach 88% by 2030. GSMA's November 2025 'Accelerating Smartphone Adoption in Africa' report gives the African-wide average as 63% in 2025, implying Nigeria's current figure is likely higher than 51%, but no more recent country-specific percentage was located within the search budget. Scored 3 (40-59%) on the most recent confirmed country figure (2022); flagged for human review since the true current-year figure may sit in the next band up (60-79%).
revised_comments: GSMA Intelligence data shows smartphone adoption in Nigeria (smartphone connections as a share of total mobile connections) at 51% in 2022, part of a rapid growth trajectory projected to reach 88% by 2030 as entry-level device prices fall and migration from feature phones to 4G/5G-capable smartphones accelerates.

Definition: The country's overall cybersecurity preparedness, based on the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI). Covers legal measures, technical measures, organisational measures, capacity development, and cooperation. Essential for trust in stored data and digital services.
Comments: Unable to locate Nigeria’s numeric ITU Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI) 2024 score in available sources; only tier reference found.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The originally cited Guardian article was fetched and confirmed accurate (Nigeria placed in GCI 2024 Tier 3), but the row was left at 0/Unknown because no numeric composite score could be found. ITU's own press release and country-tier reporting confirm Tier 3 corresponds to the 'Establishing' category, which maps to the metadata scale's GCI score band of 40-59. A score of 82.40 attributed to Nigeria by a third-party blog (Web Security Lab) is inconsistent with an official Tier 3 placement under ITU's own tier definitions (Tier 1 = Role-Modelling/highest) and was disregarded as unreliable. Score set to 3, based on ITU's own tier classification.
revised_comments: The ITU's Global Cybersecurity Index 2024 places Nigeria in Tier 3 ('Establishing'), corresponding to a GCI score in the 40-59 range. Nigeria's strongest pillar is legal measures, scoring 19.52 out of 20, underpinned by the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015 and the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation 2019, together with the ngCERT providing technical incident-response capability. Organisational measures, capacity development and international cooperation remain comparatively weaker areas.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
Comments: No authoritative nationwide residential electricity tariff vs income metric found in sources within time budget.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Fast-path check found current NERC residential tariff data (via Businessday, citing NERC directly: average allowed tariff approx. $0.07/kWh; the April 2024 service-reflective bands range from approx. ₦40-63/kWh for Bands B-E to ₦225/kWh for the most reliable Band A) but no authoritative source expresses this as a percentage of household income for a defined 'basic service' consumption level, which is what the metadata scale requires. Computing a percentage myself from tariff data and a separate GNI-per-capita estimate would rely on undocumented assumptions about 'basic service' consumption, so the row is confirmed as Unknown rather than guessed.

Definition: The number and activity level of technology hubs, incubators, accelerators, and co-working spaces focused on technology and innovation. These provide physical infrastructure and support for tech entrepreneurship and skills development.
Comments: No Nigeria-specific count of innovation hubs found from AfriLabs/Briter Bridges within available sources.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The originally cited Instagram post was fetched; it gives only a pan-African AfriLabs hub count (519 hubs across 53 countries) with no Nigeria-specific figure, so it did not support the score. A dedicated Nigerian Innovation Hub Assessment Report by the Innovation Support Network (ISN), funded by GIZ, the EU and Germany's BMZ (published May 2026), surveys 190+ actively operating hubs out of an ecosystem of 250+ active/partially-active spaces nationwide. This is corroborated by AfriLabs' own Nigeria hub directory (multiple listed hubs) and by Disrupt Africa's reporting that Nigeria is one of AfriLabs' key markets within its 496-519-hub pan-African network. Score upgraded from 0 to 5 (25+ hubs, vibrant mature ecosystem).
revised_comments: Nigeria has the largest innovation-hub ecosystem in Africa. The Innovation Support Network's 2026 national hub assessment, funded by GIZ, the EU and Germany's BMZ, identifies over 190 actively operating hubs and more than 250 active or partially active spaces nationwide, concentrated in Lagos (32% of respondents) and Abuja (16%) but present across all six geopolitical zones. Hubs focus predominantly on ICT/software development, agritech, fintech and edtech, and many are affiliated with the pan-African AfriLabs network.

Definition: The size and vibrancy of the local software developer and technology professional community. Measured through proxies such as GitHub activity, Stack Overflow representation, local tech meetup groups, and developer surveys. Indicates the country's capacity to build and maintain digital systems locally.
Comments: No credible numeric estimate (e.g., GitHub developers count) found in sourced materials; only qualitative GitHub blog/community listings available.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The originally cited sources (a 2018 GitHub blog post and an informal community-list repository) were fetched and found to be outdated or purely qualitative, unable to support a numeric score. GitHub's own Octoverse 2024 report (October 2024) records over 1.1 million developer accounts in Nigeria, up 28% year-on-year — the fastest-growing developer population among the world's most populous countries and the largest developer community in Africa, corroborated by Businessday Nigeria reporting 872,162 developers as of Q3 2023. This far exceeds the top scale threshold of 50,000+ developers. Score upgraded from 0 to 5 (Mature).
revised_comments: GitHub's Octoverse 2024 report records more than 1.1 million developer accounts in Nigeria, growing 28% year-on-year — the fastest growth rate among the world's most populous countries and the largest developer community in Africa, ahead of Egypt and South Africa. The community is supported by an established network of meetups, hackathons and training programmes (including Andela alumni networks, AI Saturdays and Google Developer Groups) concentrated in Lagos and Abuja, alongside a fast-growing base of fintech and other startups.

Definition: The proportion of the population with basic digital skills (ability to use a computer, smartphone, or the internet for simple tasks such as sending messages, finding information, or using apps). Based on ITU household survey data, Afrobarometer, or national ICT surveys.
Comments: No standard ITU 'basic digital skills' percentage located within available sources; World Bank report discusses digital skills but does not provide a single national 'basic digital skills' % metric comparable to ITU definition.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The originally cited World Bank report was fetched in full. It does not report an ITU-standard 'basic digital skills' percentage, but it does provide a usable proxy from Nigeria's 2021 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS): on average only 9% of the population used a computer in the last three months (12% of men, 6% of women), which is well within the metadata scale's <10% band. Score set to 1 rather than left at 0, since the underlying survey data does support a score.
revised_comments: Survey data from Nigeria's 2021 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), reported in the World Bank's 2024 'Digital Skills in Nigeria' policy note, shows that only around 9% of the population had used a computer in the previous three months (12% of men versus 6% of women), with usage considerably lower in rural areas (1.7% of women, 4% of men) than in urban areas (12% of women, 21% of men). Basic digital skills remain low even among wealthier and more educated groups, rising to around a third among those with tertiary education.
